# Titus 2 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## v. 1 — "But as for you, speak the things that are consistent with sound doctrine."

- **The strong contrast ("But as for you")** sets Titus apart from the false teachers described at the end of chapter 1 (Titus 1:10–16), who taught Jewish myths and commandments of men. Titus is to teach something utterly different. (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/titus-2/)
- **"Sound doctrine"** (Greek *hugiainō*) means healthy, wholesome teaching — teaching that produces spiritual health. False doctrine, by contrast, produces spiritual disease and ultimately death. Paul uses this word 9 times in the Pastoral Epistles, 5 times in Titus. (preceptaustin.org/titus_21-10)
- **The things that "befit" or "are proper for"** sound doctrine is a phrase that has to do with **right living, not just right thinking**. The NLT renders it: "Promote the kind of living that reflects right teaching." Sound doctrine is the root; godly conduct is the fruit. (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/titus-2/)
- **Gill** stresses that Titus (and all ministers) should speak these things "openly and publicly, fully and faithfully, with great plainness and evidence… constantly and continually… in season and out of season," and that the duties of religion "should be set in their true light, and proper place, as fruits of the grace of God." (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/titus/2.htm)
- **Ellicott** notes the "strictly practical nature" of Paul's charges: "Before touching upon doctrine, he presses home… the necessity of a quiet, useful life." The "sound doctrine" stands in contrast to the "sickly, unhealthy teaching, fanciful and false, of the misleading teachers of Crete." (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/titus/2.htm)
- **Precept Austin** observes that the "BUT" sets up a contrast: the false teachers "profess to know God, but by their deeds they deny Him" (Titus 1:16). One must not only speak sound doctrine but live a sound life congruent with it. To do otherwise is "to play the hypocrite." (preceptaustin.org/titus_21-10)

---

## v. 2 — "Older men are to be temperate, dignified, self-controlled, and sound in faith, love, and perseverance."

- **"Older men"** (Greek *presbutas*) means aged men in the congregation, not elders in an official sense (those were treated in chapter 1). (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/titus/2.htm; biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/titus/2.htm)
- **"Temperate"** (*nēphalios*) means sober or vigilant — watchful over conduct and conversation, lest evil be drawn into an example by younger persons. (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/titus/2.htm)
- **"Dignified"** (*semnos*) means grave, quietly earnest, with behavior, speech, and dress befitting age. Levity and frothy language are unbecoming. (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/titus/2.htm)
- **"Self-controlled"** (*sōphrōn*) means discreet or self-restrained in eating and drinking, "especially the latter, to which old age is most addicted." (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/titus/2.htm)
- **"Sound in faith, love, and perseverance"** — Paul replaces his usual triad "faith, hope, love" (1 Cor 13:13) with "faith, love, patience." Ellicott explains that "this brave patience, this enduring fortitude, especially becomes the old man waiting for death." These must be "healthy, sound" — faith not adulterated with superstitions, love not sentimental but chivalrous and broad, patience not tame acquiescence but brave endurance. (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/titus/2.htm)
- **David Guzik** notes that "patience" (*hupomonē*) means "a steadfast and active endurance, not a passive waiting. Older men are not to just patiently wait around until they pass on to the next world. They are to actively endure the challenges of life; even the challenges of old age." (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/titus-2/)
- **Gill** warns that older men, though unhealthful in body, must be sound in mind: in the doctrine of faith, in genuine love to God and His people, and in patience to bear infirmities of body and any sufferings for Christ. (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/titus/2.htm)
- **The Pulpit Commentary** warns: "We must not miss the important warning, not only to have some kind of faith, love, and patience, but to be healthy and vigorous in our faith, love, and patience. There is a puny faith, a sickly love, and a misdirected patience." (biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/titus/2.htm)

---

## v. 3 — "Older women, likewise, are to be reverent in their behavior, not slanderers or addicted to much wine, but teachers of good."

- **"Reverent in behavior"** (Greek *hieroprepeis*) — a word used only here in the NT. It means "becoming a holy person" or "suitable to a sacred office." D. Edmond Hiebert says it "conveys the image of a good priestess carrying out the duties of her office." The older woman's whole demeanor — dress, speech, bearing — is to reflect that life is sacred. (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/titus-2/)
- **John Piper (Desiring God)** elaborates: "Reverence is in accord with sound doctrine — in other words, with the gospel." A reverent woman "doesn't 'temporarily disable' God's holy presence, even for five minutes." Reverence fits redemption "like laughter fits a good joke." It involves "a steady drumbeat of repentance and faith." (desiringgod.org/articles/the-loveliness-of-reverence)
- **The Pulpit Commentary** notes that the Greek word for "demeanor" (*katastēma*) is much broader than mere dress — it includes "the movements of the body, the expression of the countenance, what is said, and what is left unsaid." St. Jerome expounded it similarly. (biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/titus/2.htm)
- **"Not slanderers"** — the Greek word is *diabolos*, the same word used for "devils." When older women slander and gossip, "they do the devils' work." (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/titus-2/)
- **"Not addicted to much wine"** — literally "not enslaved to much wine" (*douloō*). This was a common failing of older women in Roman and Greek culture; the warning was especially needed in Crete. (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/titus-2/; biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/titus/2.htm)
- **"Teachers of good"** (*kalodidaskalos*) — a unique compound word, found only here in the NT. These women teach by holy demeanor as much as by words. Ellicott notes that this does not mean public instructresses, but teaching "by here and there speaking a kind warning word, and, better still, by the golden silence of a useful honoured life." (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/titus-2/; biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/titus/2.htm)

---

## v. 4 — "In this way they can train the young women to love their husbands and children."

- **"Train"** (Greek *sōphronizō*) means to "school," "correct," "moderate," or "bring to one's senses." It is found only here in the NT. The older women are to mentor the younger in practical godliness. (biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/titus/2.htm)
- **Paul deliberately has older women teach younger women** rather than having Titus do it directly. David Guzik explains this recognizes "that this vulnerable dynamic needed wisdom and cultural sensitivity." It was dangerous for Titus to make young women a focus of his ministry. (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/titus-2/)
- **The first priority is home and family:** "to love their husbands, to love their children." Ellicott comments that in Crete there was "a feverish longing for excitement, for novelty in religious teaching," and women preferred elaborate ritual to "quietly and reverently doing their Father's business." Paul's corrective was to "recall women as well as men to the steady, faithful performance of those quiet every-day duties." (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/titus/2.htm)
- **Gill** notes that "to love their husbands" means "to help and assist them all they can; to seek their honour and interest; to endeavour to please them in all things; to secure peace, harmony, and union." It is said in opposition to "moroseness and ill nature," not merely against adultery. (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/titus/2.htm)
- **Gill on loving children:** "not with a fond, foolish, loose, and ungoverned affection; but so as to seek their real good, and not only their temporal, but spiritual and eternal welfare; to bring them up in the nurture and admonition of the Lord." (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/titus/2.htm)
- **John Piper (Desiring God):** "She loves her husband, because God has given her this one man to bless, serve, care for, and help in every way possible… She gives of herself to bless her children, even when she least feels like it, because Christ gave himself for her when she least deserved it." (desiringgod.org/articles/the-loveliness-of-reverence)

---

## v. 5 — "to be self-controlled, pure, managers of their households, kind, and submissive to their own husbands, so that the word of God will not be discredited."

- **"Self-controlled"** (*sōphrōn*) — the same word used for older men in v. 2. Discreet, wise, prudent in all conduct. (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/titus/2.htm)
- **"Pure"** (*hagnos*) — chaste not only in act but "in look, in speech, in thought, even in dress." (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/titus/2.htm)
- **"Managers of their households"** — The older manuscripts read "workers at home" (*oikourgos*) rather than "keepers at home" (*oikouros*). The meaning is little changed: "Home duties, cares, pleasures, sacrifices of self—these God-appointed duties ought to fill the mind and the heart of the young wife." Ellicott sums up: "Gute Hausfrauen will der Apostel haben" (the Apostle wants good housewives). (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/titus/2.htm)
- **Gill** quotes ancient Jewish sources that saw it as "the glory of a woman to continue at home, and not go abroad." He notes that "the tortoise, which carries its house upon its back, and very rarely shows its head, or looks out of it, was, with the ancients, an emblem of a good housewife." (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/titus/2.htm)
- **"Submissive to their own husbands"** — this echoes Ephesians 5:22 and Colossians 3:18. Ellicott notes it was especially needful in Crete, where often the Christian wife was married to a pagan husband. (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/titus/2.htm)
- **"So that the word of God will not be discredited"** — the "practical worth of a religion is not unfairly estimated by its effects on the lives of those who profess it." If the gospel made women worse wives, it would not commend itself to the heathen. (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/titus-2/, quoting Newport J.D. White)
- **Ellicott** expands: the fear was that wives "carried away by religious fervour, might neglect the plainer every-day duties for the seemingly loftier… religious works." Such failure would be bitterly charged against the religion of Christ. The reference extends to all believers: "Never should they who wear the colours of the great King forget the charge… 'Let your light so shine before men.'" (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/titus/2.htm)

---

## v. 6 — "In the same way, urge the younger men to be self-controlled."

- **"Likewise"** links the young men's instruction to what precedes. The essential message is the same for all groups, though emphasis may differ. (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/titus-2/)
- **This is the only command specifically directed to young men** in this list, but it is a comprehensive one. William Barclay says the Greek *sōphrōn* "describes the man with the mind which has everything under control… strength of mind which has learned to govern every instinct and passion until each has its proper place and no more." (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/titus-2/)
- **Ellicott** notes that the task of influencing young men belongs especially to Titus, who was still young himself (probably about 40). Chrysostom observed: "No task… is after all so hard and difficult for youth, as obtaining the mastery over oneself in the matter of harmful pleasures." (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/titus/2.htm)
- **Gill** expands "sober minded" as "temperate, chaste, modest, moderate, wise, and prudent in all things." (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/titus/2.htm)

---

## v. 7 — "In everything, show yourself to be an example by doing good works. In your teaching show integrity, dignity."

- **Titus is to be more than a teacher — he must be a "pattern" (Greek *typos*, a type or model) of good works.** His guidance to others cannot be taken seriously if he himself is not walking after the Lord. (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/titus-2/)
- **Ellicott** emphasizes: "Titus ought to be the one showing an example to the rest; in peaceful, quiet days, as in times of danger and threatening, he must set the pattern — now of useful labour and toil — now of brave, patient endurance for the Lord's sake." (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/titus/2.htm)
- **"In your teaching show integrity"** — The older manuscripts read "uncorruptness" (*aphthoria*). This refers not to the subject matter of the teaching but to the teacher's bearing: purity and freedom from all interested motives; above seeking popular applause. (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/titus/2.htm)
- **"Dignity"** (*semnotēs*) — a certain gravity in public delivery and private intercourse. Titus must never forget he is "the chief teacher in the Church of Crete of his Master's religion." (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/titus/2.htm)
- **Gill** adds that the older manuscripts omit "sincerity" (it's not in the best texts), and notes that this may either refer to doctrine delivered pure and incorrupt, or to the life of the teacher matching his doctrine. (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/titus/2.htm)
- **John Piper (Desiring God)** cites this verse in a message on being "devoted to discipline and doctrine": "In all things show yourself to be an example of good deeds, with purity in doctrine… Let's pay attention to our lives and be an example of good deeds, and have purity of doctrine." (desiringgod.org/messages/devoted-to-discipline-and-doctrine)

---

## v. 8 — "and wholesome speech that is above reproach, so that anyone who opposes us will be ashamed, having nothing bad to say about us."

- **"Sound speech"** (*logos hygiēs*) — healthy, wholesome words, in contrast to the "sickly, morbid, fanciful instruction the false teachers of Crete were in the habit of giving." The substance of teaching must be "healthy, practical, manly." (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/titus/2.htm)
- **Gill** sees this referring both to public ministry (using "wholesome words of our Lord Jesus… not in the enticing words of man's wisdom") and to private conversation ("no rotten speech, or corrupt communication… no filthiness, nor foolish talking and jesting"). (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/titus/2.htm)
- **"Having nothing bad to say about us"** — the better manuscripts read "us" (not "you"), associating Paul and the other apostles with Titus. Ellicott explains: "the evil thing which might have been said of Titus in reality would be spoken against St. Paul and the elder Apostles." The opponent will be confounded when he finds nothing bad to fairly criticise in either life or teaching. (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/titus/2.htm)
- **David Guzik** compares Jesus: "Which of you convicts Me of sin?" (John 8:46). (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/titus-2/)
- **Precept Austin** notes that "sound speech that cannot be condemned" ties back to "sound doctrine" in v. 1 — both use *hugiainō*, the healthy/wholesome word group that runs through Titus. (preceptaustin.org/titus_21-10)

---

## v. 9 — "Slaves are to submit to their own masters in everything, to be well-pleasing, not argumentative."

- **"Bondservants"** (*doulos*) is the accurate translation — this is addressed to slaves. In the ancient church, Christians shocked the larger culture by mixing slaves and masters in the social setting of worship. A slave might be an elder over his own master in the church. (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/titus-2/)
- **Spurgeon** said: "I do not think for a moment Paul believed that the practice of slavery ought to exist. He believed to the fullest extent that the great principles of Christianity would overthrow slavery anywhere, and the sooner they did so the better pleased would he be; but, for the time being, as it was the custom to have slaves, they must adorn the doctrine of God their Savior in the position in which they were." (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/titus-2/; spurgeon.org/sermons/adorning-the-gospel)
- **Ellicott** notes the repeated warnings to slaves (also Eph 6:5; Col 3:22; 1 Tim 6:1) show that "among the difficulties which Christianity had to surmount in its early years was the hard task of persuading 'the slave' that the divine Master who promised him a home… meant not that the existing relations of society should be then changed." The slave was to obey "cheerfully, willingly, without sullenness." (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/titus/2.htm)
- **"Not argumentative"** — literally "not answering again" or "not gainsaying" — not replying to masters' orders in "a pert, or saucy, or grumbling manner; an evil very incident to servants, and which greatly provokes." (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/titus/2.htm)
- **David Guzik** notes the word for "obedient" was used "to describe a company of soldiers as they stand at attention and salute their commander." (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/titus-2/)

---

## v. 10 — "not stealing from them, but showing all good faith, so that in every respect they will adorn the teaching about God our Savior."

- **"Not pilfering"** — this offence was so common in the ancient world that sometimes "servant" and "thief" were used interchangeably. Adam Clarke notes the word "signifies, not only stealing but embezzling another's property; keeping back a part of the price of any commodity sold on the master's account. In Acts 5:2, we translate it, to keep back part of the price; the crime of which Ananias and Sapphira were guilty." (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/titus-2/)
- **Ellicott** explains that many slaves were entrusted with shops or worked as artists or physicians. "A slave in the days of St. Paul had a hundred ways of showing to his owner this true and genuine fidelity, opposed to mere assumed surface obedience and service." (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/titus/2.htm)
- **"Adorn the doctrine"** — the Greek word (*kosmeō*, from which we get "cosmetics") "literally means to take precious jewels and arrange them so as to show their true beauty." (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/titus-2/)
- **Spurgeon's sermon "Adorning the Gospel"** emphasizes that the best doctrine is "eminently ethical, full of precepts and words of wisdom for daily life." He notes how Paul "continually and wisely interweaves his practical exhortations with the doctrines of religion." The gospel is adorned "when its effects on life and character are expressed in conduct." (spurgeon.org/sermons/adorning-the-gospel)
- **Calvin** remarks (as quoted by Ellicott): "it is indeed noteworthy how God deigns to receive an adornment from slaves, whose condition was so mean and abject that scarcely were they considered to rank among men at all; they were ranked as 'possessions,' just like cattle or horses." (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/titus/2.htm)
- **G. Campbell Morgan**: "While it is still only a theory doctrine lacks the manifestation of beauty. When, however, it is realized and manifested in human life its beauty at once appears." (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/titus-2/)

---

## v. 11 — "For the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation to everyone."

- **"For"** gives the theological ground for all the practical exhortations in vv. 1–10. Ellicott paraphrases: "Yes, exhort all classes and orders… for I tell you, in very truth, like a sun on a darkened world has the grace of God arisen with salvation in its beams." The Greek *epephanē* (appeared) is used of the sun's shining (Luke 1:79; Acts 27:20). (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/titus/2.htm)
- **"The grace of God"** — Gill specifies this means not the inward grace of God in the heart or God's secret love, but "the doctrine of grace, the Gospel of the grace of God… a declaration of the grace of God, and of salvation by it." That the Gospel is called "salvation itself" shows its power. (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/titus/2.htm)
- **"Bringing salvation to all men"** — Ellicott insists this does not teach universalism. It means "that grace of God whereby alone it is possible for mankind to be saved. The expression by no means asserts that all men will be saved by it, but that it is the only means by which salvation is possible." Similarly Gill: "to all sorts of men, of every nation, of every age and sex, of every state and condition, high and low, rich and poor, bond and free." (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/titus/2.htm; biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/titus/2.htm)
- **David Guzik**: "God doesn't have a gospel of grace for some and a gospel of law or self-justification for others. All men find salvation by the grace of God." (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/titus-2/)

---

## v. 12 — "It instructs us to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions, and to live sensible, upright, and godly lives in the present age."

- **"Instructs"** (Greek *paideuō*) means the full training process a parent gives a child — teaching, encouragement, correction, and discipline. Grace itself is a teacher. (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/titus-2/)
- **John Calvin**: "He means that God's grace should instruct us to order our lives aright. Some are quick to turn the preaching of God's mercy into an excuse for licentiousness… But the revelation of God's grace necessarily brings with it exhortations to a godly life." (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/titus-2/)
- **Spurgeon**: "Thus you see that grace has its own disciples. Are you a disciple of the grace of God? Did you ever come and submit yourself to it?" He also noted: "The most difficult part of the training of young men is not to put the right thing into them, but to get the wrong thing out of them." (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/titus-2/)
- **The three adverbs** — "sensibly, uprightly, and godly" — represent three spheres of life. F.B. Meyer famously said: "We are taught by that gentle school-mistress, the Grace of God, to live — soberly, as regards our personal life; righteously, in relation to others; godly, in our attitude towards God." (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/titus-2/)
- **Gill** expands "denying ungodliness" as "all impiety, or sin more immediately against God… as idolatry, will worship, superstition, perjury," and "worldly lusts" as "the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eye, and the pride of life." (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/titus/2.htm)
- **Ellicott** notes the word translated "teaching" is literally "disciplining us; educating us by life's sad experiences. God's grace is in truth a stern discipline of self-denial and training for higher things." (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/titus/2.htm)

---

## v. 13 — "as we await the blessed hope and glorious appearance of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ."

- **This is one of the strongest NT proof-texts for the deity of Christ.** The Greek construction (*tou megalou theou kai sōtēros hēmōn Iēsou Christou*) falls under **Granville Sharp's Rule**: when two personal, singular, non-proper nouns are joined by *kai* and only the first has the article, both refer to the same person. Thus "our great God and Savior" both refer to Jesus Christ — He is called "our great God." (bible.org/article/granville-sharp-model-evangelical-scholarship-and-social-activism)
- **The Granville Sharp Rule** requires: (1) both nouns are personal, (2) neither is plural, (3) neither is a proper name. Titus 2:13 meets all criteria. As A.T. Robertson concluded: "Sharp stands vindicated after all the dust has settled." (bible.org/article/granville-sharp-model-evangelical-scholarship-and-social-activism; bible.org/book/export/html/6263)
- **Catholic teaching** likewise uses this verse to demonstrate the deity of Christ, applying Granville Sharp's rule to show both "God" and "Savior" describe Jesus. (catholic.com/magazine/online-edition/how-grammar-points-to-christs-divinity; catholic.com/audio/ddp/our-god-and-savior-jesus-christ)
- **The Pulpit Commentary** notes: "This is the only place in the New Testament where *makarios* [blessed] is applied to an object which does not itself enjoy the blessing, but is a source of blessing." The hope itself is called "the blessed hope." (biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/titus/2.htm)
- **"Looking for"** (*prosdechomai*) is the word commonly used for waiting for the kingdom of God (Mark 15:43; Luke 2:25, 38; Jude 21). Christians are to live in active expectation. (biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/titus/2.htm)
- **David Guzik** elaborates the contrasts between Christ's first and second comings: "He came the first time to a tree; He will come a second time to a throne. He came the first time in humility; He will come a second time in glory." (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/titus-2/)
- **Gill** notes: "our great God and Saviour Jesus Christ… in whom we trust, and whom we expect… will certainly appear… to the salvation of his people, and to take vengeance on the wicked." He observes the phrase "our great God" is a periphrasis of the incommunicable name Jehovah. (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/titus/2.htm)

---

## v. 14 — "He gave Himself for us to redeem us from all lawlessness and to purify for Himself a people for His own possession, zealous for good deeds."

- **"He gave Himself for us"** — every word matters: "gave" (voluntary), "Himself" (all He could give), "for us" (as a substitute for sinful man). (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/titus-2/)
- **"Redeem"** (*lytroō*) means "to be bought out of slavery by the paying of a ransom." We are bought out of slavery to sin and purchased for His service. (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/titus-2/)
- **F.B. Meyer**: "We are, therefore, taught that the death of Jesus was intended, not for our forgiveness and justification merely, but for our sanctification, and our deliverance from the power of all our besetting sins." (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/titus-2/)
- **"A people for His own possession"** — the Greek word *periousios* is interesting. William Barclay explains: "It means reserved for; and it was specially used for that part of the spoils of a battle or a campaign which the king who had conquered set apart especially for himself." (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/titus-2/)
- **Gill** connects the phrase to Exodus 19:5 ("a peculiar treasure") and Deuteronomy 14:2, noting the people are "his portion and inheritance." The purification is both by the blood of Christ and by the Spirit's sanctification. (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/titus/2.htm)
- **Ellicott** continues: the redeeming and purifying are "the great objects of the atonement." Christ's death was for sanctification and deliverance from sin's power, not forgiveness only. (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/titus/2.htm)
- **"Zealous for good deeds"** — we are redeemed to live with zeal. This zeal is with knowledge, and zeal for righteousness in one's own life before zeal for righteousness in others' lives. (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/titus-2/)

---

## v. 15 — "Speak these things as you encourage and rebuke with all authority. Let no one despise you."

- **"Speak, exhort, and rebuke"** — three aspects of the preacher's task: declarative teaching, positive encouragement, and corrective rebuke — all done "with all authority" (*epitagē*, implying a command). God's messengers are messengers from a King. (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/titus-2/)
- **"Let no one despise you"** — Hiebert notes that "since this letter would be read in the churches, the remark was apparently intended as much for the Cretans as for Titus himself." Titus must back up his authority with his life so that no one would despise him or his message. (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/titus-2/)
- **Gill**: Titus was to "let no man despise his youth, or detract from his authority, or make light of his doctrine and exhortations." He should carry himself with gravity, act with boldness, and not give occasion for contempt. (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/titus/2.htm)
- **Ellicott** adds that Titus must "urge these lessons of the true discipline of the Christian life which spring out of the real doctrine of the cross." The authority is not personal but derives from the message itself. (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/titus/2.htm)

---

## Denominational Distinctives

### v. 5 — "Keepers at home" / "Workers at home" — Complementarian vs. Egalitarian Readings

- **Complementarian (traditional) reading:** Held consistently by **Reformed (Ligonier), Baptist (Desiring God, GTY), and many conservative Presbyterian** sources. The wife's primary God-given sphere is the home; submission to the husband is a creation ordinance that reflects Christ and the church (Eph 5:22–33). The phrase "keepers at home" is understood as a positive command for married women to prioritize domestic responsibilities, not as a prohibition against all work outside the home, but as setting the home as the primary focus. (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/titus-2/; desiringgod.org/articles/the-loveliness-of-reverence; biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/titus/2.htm)
- **Egalitarian reading:** Some modern evangelical and progressive scholars argue that "workers at home" (the better-attested reading) does not prohibit women from working outside the home or holding leadership positions. They contend Paul was addressing a specific cultural situation in Crete, not establishing a timeless universal prohibition. (This perspective is found in some modern commentary but was not directly represented in the sites searched.)
- **Methodist/Wesleyan tradition:** Historically, the Holiness movement produced many female preachers and leaders (Phoebe Palmer, Catherine Booth). However, Wesley's own notes tend to affirm the plain sense of the text, and modern Wesleyan denominations are divided. (Specific Wesleyan sources on this verse were not retrieved in the searches.)

### v. 13 — "Our great God and Savior Jesus Christ" — Deity of Christ

- **Reformed, Baptist, Lutheran, Pentecostal, and virtually all orthodox Protestant traditions** affirm this verse teaches the full deity of Christ via Granville Sharp's Rule. The grammar requires that "God" and "Savior" refer to the same person — Jesus Christ. (bible.org/article/granville-sharp-model-evangelical-scholarship-and-social-activism)
- **Catholic teaching** agrees entirely, using the same grammatical argument. (catholic.com/magazine/online-edition/how-grammar-points-to-christs-divinity)
- **Orthodox** teaching also affirms this verse as a Christological proof-text. (Specific OCA.org sources were not retrieved, but Eastern Orthodox theology strongly affirms Christ's deity.)
- **Jehovah's Witnesses (NWT)** translates this verse as "of the great God and of our Savior Jesus Christ," inserting "of" before "Savior" to separate the two, but this violates Granville Sharp's Rule and is widely rejected by Greek scholars. (This was not directly from the allowed sites but is a well-known difference.)

### v. 11 — "Has appeared to all men" — Extent of Grace

- **Calvinist/Reformed:** Interpret "all men" as "all sorts of men" (not every individual without exception). Gill is explicit: "to all sorts of men, of every nation, of every age and sex, of every state and condition." The gospel has appeared to all nations, not just Jews. (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/titus/2.htm)
- **Arminian/Wesleyan/Methodist:** Tend to see "all men" as affirming universal provision of grace (prevenient grace), available to every person, though not all receive it. (Specific Wesleyan sources were not retrieved in searches.)
- **Lutheran:** Typically holds to universal objective justification — Christ died for all — while distinguishing this from subjective reception by faith. "All men" affirms the universality of the offer. (Specific LCMS sources not retrieved.)

## Other Views

### Catholic Reading

- **New Advent / Catholic Answers** affirms Titus 2:13 as a key proof-text for Christ's divinity, applying Granville Sharp's Rule. The Catholic reading is largely identical to the conservative Protestant reading on the Christological significance of this verse. (catholic.com/magazine/online-edition/how-grammar-points-to-christs-divinity)
- Catholic moral theology shares with the traditional Protestant reading the emphasis on the domestic virtues and the orderly household as reflecting the order of creation and the Church. (Specific verse-by-verse Catholic commentary on all of Titus 2 was not retrieved from newadvent.org.)

- **On slavery (vv. 9–10):** Modern scholars often note that Paul was not endorsing the institution of slavery but "regulating an existing institution" within a first-century context where immediate abolition was not feasible. The seeds of slavery's undoing are planted in verses like Galatians 3:28 and Philemon.

### Hyper-Grace / Word of Faith

- **No direct sources** from the approved list addressed hyper-grace or Word of Faith readings of Titus 2. However, it is well known that **hyper-grace teachers** sometimes pit the grace of v. 11 against the ethical instructions of vv. 1–10, arguing that emphasizing moral duties undermines grace. The traditional response, from all the sources reviewed, is that **grace itself teaches godly living** (v. 12) — the two are inseparable. Spurgeon forcefully stated: "Wherever the grace of God comes effectually, it makes the loose liver deny the desires of the flesh… Not only do we leave these lusts, but we deny them." (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/titus-2/)
